sentences.text: Bori wrote hers on the eighteenth of October in a temper, at half past nine at night, sitting on her bed with the door shut.
It was about Emese.

Emese had been her friend since they were four and had started at the gimnázium in Kecskemét in September, which meant the bus at ten past six and back at seven, and which meant that Emese now had a whole life seven hours a day that Bori was not in.
That was not the problem.
Bori had understood about the bus.

The problem was a thing Emese had said on the Sunday, at the shop, in front of two girls from Kecskemét, which was not cruel and was not even untrue and which had been said in a particular voice — a slightly amused, slightly explaining voice — and which had made Bori, for about four seconds, into somebody being described rather than somebody standing there.
Emese had almost certainly not noticed doing it.
That was the worst part.
Bori had watched her not notice.

That was the thing she could not get past: she had watched Emese's face for the whole four seconds, hoping to find something in it, and there had been nothing there at all — just Emese, being funny in a shop, in a good mood, with two new people she liked.

Bori had gone over it about two hundred times by Wednesday and was completely certain that if she said anything, Emese would be baffled, and would apologise, and would mean it, and would not understand, and then Bori would have spent the thing and got nothing.
So she wrote it.
She wrote about a page.
She was not proud of the middle section then and is not now.

She said the thing about the voice, and then she said several other things that had been sitting underneath it since about March, and one of them was true and specific and would have ended it between them for good.
She folded it once and went out in the dark and put it in the hollow in the wall by the chapel, and came back in and slept better than she had in a fortnight.
That is the part she wants understood.
She slept well.
She was not tormented; she did not lie awake regretting it.
She had done the thing you are supposed to do with an unsayable thing, and she had done it properly, and she had felt the exact relief her grandmother had described.
The date was the eighteenth.
The geese came on the twenty-first, every year, give or take a day.
She had three days.
The geese came that night.
They were three days early.

They had not been three days early in living memory — there was an argument about 1974 that nobody could settle — and Bori woke at some time after midnight to the dogs going and the sound of a room full of people shaking out sheets, going over low, for a long time.
She sat up in bed in the dark with her heart hammering and understood, before she was properly awake, exactly what she had done.
She got as far as the top of the stairs.
The rule about not going out is not enforced by anything.
There is no penalty and there is no watchman and her parents were asleep.
She stood at the top of the stairs in the dark for the length of the whole flight-over, with her hand on the rail, listening to the wingbeats going over the roof, and she did not go down.

She has never been able to decide whether that was obedience or cowardice or the first genuinely adult decision of her life, and she suspects it was all three and that they are frequently the same thing.
